brief.topic: Does chewing hard gum build a sharper jawline
brief.readerQuestion: Does chewing hard gum (like Falim or Mastic gum) actually give you a sharper jawline?

claims.statement: In a 6-month randomized trial in healthy adults, chewing gum three times a day did not significantly change masseter thickness or mandibular shape compared with baseline.

evidence.quote: There was no statistically significant difference in MMT or mandibular shape compared to the baseline.

claims.statement: Gum chewing training does increase bite force in healthy adults. The strength gain was seen in a 6-month RCT and also in a small trial of hard gum.

evidence.quote: Mastication training using gum increases maximum occlusal force due to an increase in occlusal contact area but has no effect on MMT or mandibular shape.
In conclusion, 4 weeks training with a hard chewing gum seems to influence the functional capacity of the masticatory muscles and increase their strength.

claims.statement: Stronger bite force from chewing hard gum is a functional change. These studies don't show it makes the jaw look bigger or more defined. In the 6-month RCT, bite force rose while masseter thickness and jaw shape did not change.

evidence.quote: The mean maximum occlusal force of the training group at 3 months was significantly higher than that at baseline, which was also significantly different from that in the control group (p < .001).

claims.statement: One month of gum chewing training changed how oxygen is used in the masseter muscle and improved its aerobic capacity. This was a very small trial (16 people) that measured muscle physiology, not appearance.

evidence.quote: In conclusion, 1 month of GCh training changed masseter oxygen dynamics during clenching and recovery and improved muscle aerobic capacity.

claims.statement: A small cross-sectional study of young adults found no statistically significant link between gum-chewing frequency, duration or chronicity and temporomandibular disorders. The study was underpowered and can't show causation, so it doesn't prove heavy chewing is safe.

evidence.quote: No statistically significant associations were found between TMD occurrence and the frequency, duration, or chronicity of gum chewing (p > 0.05).

advice: Don't count on hard gum to sharpen your jawline. The best trial found no change in jaw shape.
If you try gum anyway, stop if you get jaw pain, clicking, locking or headaches, and see a dentist or TMD specialist.
Jaw definition mostly depends on body fat, bone structure and dental or skeletal alignment. A dentist, orthodontist or maxillofacial surgeon can assess your bite and facial structure.
Don't use extremely hard or non-food chewing products in place of professional advice if you already have jaw problems.

# Does Hard Gum Actually Build a Better Jawline?

If you've spent any time in mewing and jaw-training threads, you've seen the pitch: chew hard gum, work the masseters, get a sharper jaw. Some of that holds up. The part you actually care about mostly doesn't. Here's what the trials show.

## Yes, your bite gets stronger

Chewing gum as training does increase bite force in healthy adults. A 6-month RCT showed it, and so did a small trial of hard gum. [PMID:39215439] [PMID:7709901]

The hard gum trial was short, only four weeks, but its authors concluded the training seemed to influence the functional capacity of the masticatory muscles and increase their strength. [PMID:7709901]

If your goal is "my jaw muscles can produce more force," the evidence says gum can do that.

## Stronger is not bigger, and it's not sharper

Bite force is a functional change. In the 6-month RCT, the training group's maximum bite force ended up significantly higher than at baseline and higher than the control group's. [PMID:39215439] But masseter thickness and jaw shape didn't change. [PMID:39215439]

So the best trial we have shows people getting stronger without getting a different-looking jaw. If you were hoping the trial would show a masseter bulking up and carving out an angle, it didn't.

This is also the main reason to be skeptical of before-and-after photos from gum routines. Lighting, weight changes, and head angle can account for a lot. The one controlled trial that measured shape found none.

## The muscle does adapt, just not visibly (as far as we know)

A one-month gum chewing trial changed how oxygen is used in the masseter during clenching and recovery, and it improved the muscle's aerobic capacity. [PMID:39400843] That sounds promising until you check the details: it was a very small trial of 16 people, and it measured muscle physiology, not appearance. [PMID:39400843]

So the muscle adapts in ways you can measure with the right equipment. That doesn't mean the adaptation shows up in the mirror, and nothing in these trials claims it does.

## What about wrecking your jaw joint?

This is the other question in every thread: does heavy chewing mess up your TMJ? A small cross-sectional study of young adults found no statistically significant link between gum-chewing frequency, duration, or chronicity and temporomandibular disorders (TMD). [PMID:40806875]

Don't read that as a green light. The study was underpowered and can't show causation, so it doesn't prove heavy chewing is safe. [PMID:40806875] "We didn't detect a link in a small sample" is a different statement from "there's no risk." If you're pushing hard gum for hours a day, you're running your own experiment with no safety data behind you.

## What to do with this

**Don't count on hard gum to sharpen your jawline.** The best trial found no change in jaw shape. If you chew gum anyway because you like it or want the bite-strength gain, fine. Just don't expect a new face.

**If you try it, know when to stop.** Quit if you get jaw pain, clicking, locking, or headaches, and see a dentist or TMD specialist. Those are your cues to stop experimenting.

**If you already have jaw problems, skip the DIY.** Don't use extremely hard or non-food chewing products in place of professional advice. That includes the "jaw trainer" stuff that gets marketed as a shortcut.

**Look at what actually drives jaw definition.** It mostly comes down to body fat, bone structure, and dental or skeletal alignment. Two of those you can't change with a snack, and the third you can change with a long-term, boring plan.

- **Body fat:** This is the lever most guys can pull. If your jaw looks soft, the issue may be what's covering it, not what's underneath.
- **Bone structure:** Fixed unless you go the surgical route, which is a conversation with a professional, not a forum.
- **Alignment:** Your bite and how your teeth and jaws line up are things a professional can assess.

**Get your structure assessed by someone qualified.** A dentist, orthodontist, or maxillofacial surgeon can evaluate your bite and facial structure. That's a more useful answer than another thread of strangers guessing from a photo. If something about your bite or jaw bugs you, they can tell you whether it's an alignment issue, a structural one, or just normal variation.

## Bottom line

Gum chewing training makes your bite stronger. That's supported. It also changed masseter oxygen use in a tiny one-month trial. [PMID:39400843] What the evidence doesn't show is a bigger masseter or a reshaped jaw, which is what most people are chewing for. [PMID:39215439]

If you like gum, chew gum. If you want a different jawline, put your effort into body composition and get a professional opinion on your bite and structure. That's less exciting than a jaw hack, but it's where the evidence points.
